Q122820005.summary: Christ sits at the top centre, haloed and raising both hands in blessing, as a dense crowd presses around him; below, figures bend over the gathered food and a large basket fills the foreground. The heavy, strongly modelled figures fill the panel so completely that little of the openwork ground remains. Part of the Magdeburg ivories made for Otto I's new archbishopric, the plaque celebrates Christ who feeds the multitude.
facts: The Louvre owns two of the sixteen surviving Magdeburg ivories; this one was given by a group of Friends of the Louvre in 1909.
Its history runs from Magdeburg Cathedral, probably via the Halle treasury, to the collections of Girolamo Possenti in Fabriano (sold 1880), Sigismond Bardac and Edouard Larcade.
Wikipedia's list of the plaques (after Fillitz) identifies the scene as the second miracle of the loaves and fishes, the feeding of the four thousand.
Q122820005.notes: Inv. OA 6310. The Louvre title does not specify which feeding is shown; the scripture follows the identification as the second (four thousand) feeding.
Q122820005.original_title: Plaque : Multiplication des pains et des poissons

cur:manuscripts-rossano-entry-jerusalem.summary: Christ, haloed in gold and seated sideways on a dark donkey, rides with his disciples behind him toward the gate of Jerusalem, while men cut branches from a tree and spread garments in his path and children come out from the city to greet him. Below, four Old Testament prophets in half-length raise their hands toward the scene above, pointing to the fulfilment of their words. It is one of the earliest surviving painted narratives of Palm Sunday.
facts: The Rossano Gospels is a Greek Gospel book written in silver ink on purple-dyed parchment; it was discovered in 1846 in the cathedral of Rossano in Calabria.
Its picture cycle is arranged not in Gospel order but according to the readings of Lent and Holy Week, with prophets below each scene pointing up to the New Testament events they foretold.

cur:manuscripts-rossano-entry-jerusalem.notes: Folio numbers follow the conventional numbering of the miniature leaves (1r Lazarus, 1v Entry ... 8v Barabbas); the museum lists the miniatures in this order without folio numbers.

walters:71.142.summary: In the upper scene Christ hangs on the cross beneath its titulus, flanked by the Virgin and St John and by the soldiers Longinus and Stephaton, while a coiled serpent at the foot of the cross stands for conquered evil. Below, an angel seated before the empty tomb greets the holy women; the tomb is carved as a tall, domed building recalling the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. Death and Resurrection are joined on a single plaque made to adorn the cover of a Gospel book.
facts: The Walters dates the plaque to about 870–880, in the reign of Charles the Bald, grandson of Charlemagne.
It is said to come from the Abbey of Maroilles in northern France, and was bought by Henry Walters in 1926.
The small holes around the border are where the plaque was once fixed to a book cover.
